newsitem.title: UK: Sunshine brings British voters out in millions.
newsitem.headline: Sunshine brings British voters out in millions.

text.p: Britons voted in their millions on Thursday in an election that could end 18 years in the political wilderness for the rejuvenated Labour Party.
The warmest day of the year attracted a brisk turnout and security forces were put on high alert in case Irish Republican Army guerrillas launched a polling day attack.
Opinion polls all pointed to victory for Labour leader Tony Blair, a telegenic modernist who dumped much of the party's socialist dogma in a bid to woo the middle class votes he needs for victory.
But Prime Minister John Major surprised the pundits with a shock victory in 1992 and this time he constantly criss-crossed Britain for the longest election campaign of the last 80 years.
A quarter of the population are too young to remember what life was like before "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher swept to power in 1979 and transformed Britain into a free enterprise powerhouse.
A record 3,717 candidates are standing for 659 seats, eight more than in 1992 because of boundary changes.
Polling officials reported that turnout was brisk across the country on a sunny May Day. There are 44 million eligible voters.
Security was heavy to combat any attempt by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to disrupt the voting as it has done in the six-week campaign with a string of bombs and hoaxes.
Voters were warned their bags might be searched because of the IRA threat but voters at polling stations in and around London said there were few signs of unusual security.
The Home Office (interior ministry) has sent leaflets to 45,000 electoral officers advising how to cope with bomb threats. If necessary, voting would be continued on Friday.
The IRA wants to oust Britain from Northern Ireland. Its political arm Sinn Fein hopes to win three constituencies but would refuse to take its seats in the London parliament.
In Northern Ireland, polling was delayed by security alerts involving abandoned vehicles. Belfast City Airport had to be closed but no bombs were found.
Share prices in London, fuelled by a buoyant Wall Street, closed at a record high. Now traders are keeping a wary eye on the size of Labour's expected majority.
All three political leaders voted early in their constituencies before returning to London for the result.

Major, dressed in Conservative blue tie, shirt and suit, looked relaxed when he voted in his constituency of Huntingdon, north of London, with his wife Norma. "It's now for the people to make up their minds," he told reporters.

Blair and his wife Cherie took their three young children to the polling station in Sedgefield, north-east England, giving them a glimpse of the media frenzy that awaits them if they change homes to Downing Street on Friday.
Blair, in shirt sleeves, crossed a soccer pitch belonging to a local coal mine for one last photo-call before voting.
He looked nervous and when asked if he felt like a prime minister, he said only: "That depends on the people."
Blair became a member of parliament in 1983 and will be Britain's youngest prime minister this century if he wins. He was a student at Oxford University when Labour last won a British election.
Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown, on his way to vote in Yeovil, south-western England, suffered the indignity of being nipped by a Jack Russell terrier.

Early voters at one polling station near Nottingham had to cast their votes in a car -- officials set up the makeshift polling station after a mix-up with the building caretaker over the centre's keys.
